name: Otak-otak
history: Otak-otak is a fragrant Southeast Asian fish paste mixed with coconut milk and spices, wrapped in leaves and grilled or steamed. Malaysian versions often have a soft, custardy centre.
servingSuggestions: Serve warm in the opened leaf with cucumber and sambal.
ingredients: Fish sauce and palm sugar – 1 tablespoon each
instructions: Blend fish, coconut milk, curry paste, eggs, lemongrass, fish sauce and sugar into a coarse paste.
Fold through finely shredded lime leaf and chill for 20 minutes.
Soften banana leaves over heat, spoon on the paste and secure each parcel.
Grill over medium heat or steam until the centre is opaque and safely cooked, about 12–15 minutes.

name: Sklandrausis
history: Sklandrausis is a Latvian rye tart with layered potato and sweet carrot fillings, finished with caraway and sour cream. Its raised folded rim gives the protected regional speciality its distinctive shape.
servingSuggestions: Cool to room temperature and serve with milk, tea or honey.
ingredients: Sugar, caraway and salt – to taste
instructions: Make a firm dough with the flours, butter, salt and enough warm water; rest for 20 minutes.
Boil potatoes and carrots separately and mash each smooth.
Season potato with salt and sour cream; season carrot with sugar, egg, caraway and sour cream.
Shape thin dough discs with raised rims, add potato then carrot filling.
Bake at 190°C for 20–25 minutes until the rye base is crisp.

name: Yomari
history: Yomari are Newar steamed rice-flour dumplings shaped like tapered figs and filled with warm chaku molasses and sesame. They are central to the Yomari Punhi festival.
servingSuggestions: Serve hot after steaming, with tea and extra toasted sesame.
ingredients: Chaku molasses or dark jaggery – 220 g
instructions: Melt molasses gently with ghee, sesame, coconut and cardamom; cool until thick.
Mix rice flour and salt, then add hot water gradually and knead into a smooth warm dough.
With wet hands form a cone, hollow the centre and thin the walls carefully.
Fill with molasses mixture and pinch the opening closed into a pointed shape.
Steam on a lined tray for 12–15 minutes until glossy and cooked through.

name: Canederli
history: Canederli are Alpine bread dumplings from northern Italy, made from stale bread, milk, egg and often speck. They are served in broth or with butter and cheese.
servingSuggestions: Serve in clear beef broth or drained with browned butter, chives and Parmesan.
ingredients: Stale white bread – 350 g, small cubes
Speck or smoked bacon – 150 g, diced
Nutmeg, salt and black pepper – to taste
instructions: Soak bread in warm milk for 15 minutes without making it wet enough to collapse.
Cook speck and onion until fragrant and cool slightly.
Mix bread, eggs, speck, herbs, flour and seasoning; rest for 15 minutes.
Shape with wet hands and test one dumpling in gently simmering salted water.
Adjust with flour if needed, then simmer the remaining dumplings for about 15 minutes.

name: Banosh
history: Banosh is a Hutsul Carpathian cornmeal dish cooked with sour cream until silky, then topped with bryndza cheese, mushrooms or crisp pork.
servingSuggestions: Serve immediately with bryndza, fried mushrooms and bacon cracklings.
instructions: Fry bacon until crisp, then brown mushrooms in the rendered fat and keep warm.
Bring sour cream, water and salt to a gentle simmer in a heavy pan.
Rain in cornmeal while whisking constantly to prevent lumps.
Cook over low heat, stirring, until thick and glossy and the grain is tender.
Beat in butter and top with cheese, bacon and mushrooms.

name: Num banh chok
history: Num banh chok is Cambodia's breakfast rice noodle dish, covered with a fragrant green fish gravy made with lemongrass, turmeric and coconut, then piled with raw herbs and vegetables.
servingSuggestions: Arrange herbs, cucumber, banana blossom and lime at the table for diners to add freely.
ingredients: Garlic, shallots and galangal – 100 g combined
Cucumber, bean sprouts, herbs and lime – to serve
instructions: Poach fish in lightly salted water until just cooked; flake carefully and reserve the broth.
Pound lemongrass, turmeric, lime leaf, garlic, shallot and galangal into a fine paste.
Cook the paste until fragrant, add fish, coconut milk and enough broth for a pourable gravy.
Simmer gently for 20 minutes and adjust salt and sweetness.
Divide noodles among bowls, ladle over hot gravy and add fresh vegetables and herbs.

name: Ndolé
history: Ndolé is Cameroon's celebrated bitterleaf stew, thickened with ground peanuts and enriched with beef, smoked fish or prawns. Careful washing balances the leaf's pleasant bitterness.
servingSuggestions: Serve with boiled plantain, miondo cassava sticks or rice.
ingredients: Smoked fish – 200 g, checked for bones
Oil, chilli, salt and stock – as needed
instructions: Wash and blanch bitterleaf repeatedly until the bitterness is balanced, then squeeze dry.
Simmer beef with onion and seasoning until tender, reserving the stock.
Boil peanuts until soft and blend with stock into a smooth paste.
Cook peanut paste with beef, smoked fish and bitterleaf over low heat, stirring frequently.
Sauté prawns separately, fold them in at the end and cook until opaque.

name: Zigni
history: Zigni is an Eritrean slow-cooked beef stew with a concentrated onion base, berbere and tomatoes. Long cooking softens both meat and spice into a rich sauce for injera.
servingSuggestions: Spoon over injera with lentils, greens and fresh salad.
ingredients: Niter kibbeh or clarified butter – 80 g
instructions: Cook onions dry over medium-low heat until collapsed and lightly coloured.
Add niter kibbeh, berbere, garlic and cardamom and cook gently until aromatic.
Add beef and turn it in the spice base, then add tomatoes and a small amount of water.
Cover and simmer slowly for 75–90 minutes, stirring and adding water only as needed.
Cook until beef is tender and the sauce thick and glossy, then adjust salt.

name: Asam pedas
history: Asam pedas is a Malaysian sour-hot fish stew whose chilli paste is sharpened with tamarind and scented with torch ginger and laksa leaf.
servingSuggestions: Serve with steamed rice, cucumber and a simple omelette.
ingredients: Laksa leaves, turmeric, oil, salt and sugar – as needed
instructions: Blend chillies, shallots, lemongrass and turmeric into a smooth paste.
Fry the paste in oil until darker and the oil begins to separate.
Add tamarind water, tomato, torch ginger and enough water for a light gravy; simmer 10 minutes.
Add fish and okra and simmer gently without vigorous stirring until the fish is safely cooked.
Balance the sauce with salt and a little sugar and finish with laksa leaves.

name: Mie Aceh
history: Mie Aceh is a robust Acehnese noodle dish shaped by local, Indian and Middle Eastern spice traditions. Thick yellow noodles are cooked dry, wet or soupy with a fragrant curry base.
servingSuggestions: Serve with pickled shallots, cucumber, lime, fried shallots and emping crackers.
ingredients: Ground cumin, coriander and fennel – 1 teaspoon each
Soy sauce, stock, spring onion, lime and chilli – as needed
instructions: Blend shallots, garlic and chilli and fry with curry powder and ground spices until fragrant.
Add the chosen protein and cook until nearly done, then add tomato and cabbage.
Add noodles, soy sauce and 250–500 ml stock depending on whether a dry or soupy version is desired.
Toss or simmer until noodles absorb the spice base and the protein is safely cooked.
Finish with spring onion and lime and serve with the traditional garnishes.
